title: Big Orders with Customer Names
prompt:
Tables `customers(id, name)` and `orders(id, customer_id, amount)`.

Return the order `id`, the customer's `name`, and the `amount` for every order with `amount` greater than 100.
hint: JOIN orders to customers on customer_id = customers.id, filter amount > 100.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER);

title: Top Earner in Each Department
prompt:
Table `employees(id, name, dept, salary)`. Assume no salary ties within a department.

Return the `dept` and `name` of the highest-paid employee in each department.
hint: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC), then filter rank = 1.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept TEXT, salary INTEGER);

title: Authors With Unreviewed Books
prompt: A bookstore tracks authors, the books they wrote, and reader reviews left on individual books. The authors table has id and name. The books table has id, title, and author_id (the author who wrote it). The reviews table has id, book_id (the book being reviewed), and rating. List the name of every author who has written at least one book that has never received a review. Return distinct author names, ordered alphabetically.
hint: Join authors to books, then LEFT JOIN reviews and keep rows where the review is missing.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE authors (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE books (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, author_id INTEGER); CREATE TABLE reviews (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, book_id INTEGER, rating INTEGER);

List the name of every employee assigned to more than one distinct project, along with the count of distinct projects they're assigned to. title: Instructors Teaching Multiple Departments
prompt: An instructors table has columns id and name. A course_sections table has columns id, instructor_id, department, and enrolled. Find instructors who teach sections in at least 2 different departments and whose total enrollment across all their sections exceeds 100. Return the instructor name, distinct department count, and total enrollment, ordered by total enrollment from highest to lowest, then by instructor name alphabetically for ties.
hint: Combine COUNT(DISTINCT department) with SUM(enrolled) in the same HAVING clause.
schema_sql:
CREATE TABLE instructors (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE course_sections (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, instructor_id INTEGER, department TEXT, enrolled INTEGER);

title: Products Priced Above Their Category Average
prompt: A products table lists each product's id, name, category, and price. Find every product whose price is strictly higher than the average price of all products in its own category. Return the product's name, category, and price, ordered by name.
hint: In the WHERE clause, compare each product's price against a subquery that averages prices for rows sharing its category.

title: Students Who Passed Every Exam They Took
prompt: A students table lists each student's id and name. An exam_scores table records each exam a student took, with student_id, exam_name, and score (0-100). A passing score is 60 or above. Find every student who took at least one exam and never scored below 60 on any exam. Return the student's name, ordered by name.
hint: Combine an EXISTS check for having taken an exam with a NOT EXISTS check for any exam scored below the passing mark.

title: The Second-Newest Order for Each Customer
prompt: An orders table records each order's id, customer_name, order_date (text, 'YYYY-MM-DD'), and amount. No customer places two orders on the same date. For each customer who has placed at least two orders, find their second most recent order (the one immediately before their newest). Return customer_name, order_date, and amount, ordered by customer_name.
hint: For each order, count how many of that customer's other orders have a later date, then keep rows where that count is exactly 1.

title: Suppliers With No Late Deliveries
prompt: A suppliers table lists each supplier's id and name. A deliveries table records each delivery's id, supplier_id, and is_late (1 if the delivery was late, 0 otherwise). Find every supplier who has made at least one delivery and has never made a late one. Return the supplier's name, ordered by name.
hint: Pair an EXISTS check for having any delivery with a NOT EXISTS check for a late one from the same supplier.

title: Customers Who Ordered in Two Different Months
prompt: An orders table records each order's id, customer_name, and order_date (text, 'YYYY-MM-DD'). Find every customer who has placed orders in at least two different calendar months (the year is ignored, only the month matters). Return each qualifying customer_name once, ordered by customer_name.
hint: For each order, check with EXISTS whether the same customer has another order whose month portion differs from this one's.

title: Branches Outperforming Their Region's Average Revenue
prompt: A branches table lists each branch's id, name, region, and revenue. Find every branch whose revenue is strictly higher than the average revenue of all branches in its own region. Return the branch's name, region, and revenue, ordered by region then name.
hint: Compare each branch's revenue against a subquery averaging revenue over branches that share its region.

title: Movies Rated Above the Director's Other Films
prompt: A movies table lists each movie's id, title, director, and rating. Find every movie whose rating is strictly higher than the average rating of that same director's other movies (excluding the movie itself). A director with only one movie has no 'other movies' and cannot qualify. Return the movie's title, director, and rating, ordered by director then title.
hint: The averaging subquery must correlate on both the director and exclude the current row's own id.

title: Warehouses That Never Ran Out of Stock
prompt: A warehouses table lists each warehouse's id and name. A stock_checks table records each inventory check's id, warehouse_id, check_date, and quantity on hand at that time. Find every warehouse that has had at least one stock check and was never recorded with a quantity of 0. Return the warehouse's name, ordered by name.
hint: Require EXISTS at least one stock check for the warehouse and NOT EXISTS one where quantity equals 0.

title: Employees With the Longest Tenure in Their Department
prompt: An employees table lists each employee's id, name, department, and hire_date (text, 'YYYY-MM-DD'; earlier means longer tenure). Find the employee(s) in each department with the earliest hire_date - if two employees in the same department share the earliest date, include both. Return name, department, and hire_date, ordered by department then name.
hint: An employee qualifies when no other employee in the same department has an earlier hire_date - express that with NOT EXISTS.

title: Customers Whose Orders Never Dipped Below Fifty Dollars
prompt: An orders table records each order's id, customer_name, and amount. Find every customer who has placed at least one order and whose orders were all for $50 or more (never below $50). Return each qualifying customer_name once, ordered by customer_name.
hint: A customer qualifies when there is NOT EXISTS an order of theirs with amount less than 50.

title: Products That Have Never Been Returned
prompt: A products table lists each product's id and name. A returns table records each returned item's id, product_id, and return_date. Find every product that has never appeared in the returns table. Return the product's name, ordered by name.
hint: Use NOT EXISTS against the returns table, correlating on product_id.

title: Salespeople Who Beat Their Previous Quarter
prompt: A quarterly_sales table records each sales rep's revenue for a given quarter, with columns id, rep_name, quarter (a sequential integer, 1, 2, 3, ...), and revenue. Find every rep/quarter row where that quarter's revenue is strictly higher than the same rep's revenue in the immediately preceding quarter (quarter - 1). Rows with no matching prior-quarter record for that rep don't qualify. Return rep_name, quarter, and revenue, ordered by rep_name then quarter.
hint: Use a correlated subquery that fetches the same rep's revenue where quarter equals the outer row's quarter minus 1.

title: Runner-Up Sale in Each Region
prompt: A retailer logs individual sales in a table named sales with columns id, region, salesperson, and amount (each row is one sale). For each region, find the sale with the second-highest amount (the runner-up sale). Regions with fewer than two sales have no runner-up and should not appear in the result. Return region, salesperson, and amount, ordered by region ascending.
hint: Number the sales within each region by amount descending and keep only the row numbered 2.

title: Most Recent Login Per User
prompt: A logins table records every sign-in event with columns id, username, and login_at (a timestamp stored as text, e.g. '2026-01-03 09:00:00'). A user may sign in many times. For each username, find their most recent login_at. Return username and login_at, ordered by username ascending.
hint: Number each user's logins by login_at descending and keep only the first-numbered row per user.

title: Top Three Rated Movies in Each Genre
prompt: A movies table has columns id, title, genre, and rating. For each genre, find the movies whose rating places them in the top 3 distinct rating tiers, where tied ratings share the same tier so that no movie belonging to a top-3 rating is dropped because of an arbitrary tie-break (for example, if two movies tie for the second-best rating in a genre, both are included). Return genre, title, and rating, ordered by genre ascending, then rating descending, then title ascending.
hint: Use a dense rank of rating within each genre and keep rows where that rank is 3 or less.

title: First Purchase Date Per Customer
prompt: A purchases table records every order with columns id, customer, purchase_date (text, e.g. '2026-01-05'), and amount. For each customer, find the date of their very first purchase. Return customer and purchase_date, ordered by customer ascending.
hint: Number each customer's purchases by purchase_date ascending and keep the row numbered 1.

title: Second-Highest Distinct Score Per Student and Subject
prompt: A school records every exam attempt in exam_scores with columns id, student, subject, and score. A student may attempt the same subject's exam more than once, sometimes scoring the same value twice. For each student-subject pair, find their second-highest distinct score (so if a student scored 90 twice and 85 once, the second-highest distinct score is 85, not 90 again). Student-subject pairs with fewer than two distinct scores should not appear in the result. Return student, subject, and score, ordered by student ascending then subject ascending.
hint: Dense-rank each student-subject group's scores descending so equal scores share a rank, then keep rank 2.

title: Ranking Sprinters by Finish Time in Each Heat
prompt: A heat_results table records race results with columns id, heat, sprinter, and finish_seconds. Within each heat, rank the sprinters from fastest (lowest finish_seconds) to slowest using standard competition ranking: sprinters tied on finish_seconds share the same rank, and the next distinct time skips ranks accordingly (two sprinters tied for 1st means the next sprinter is ranked 3rd). Return heat, sprinter, finish_seconds, and the rank, ordered by heat ascending, then rank ascending, then sprinter ascending.
hint: This is exactly what the RANK window function does when ordered by finish_seconds ascending within each heat.

title: Latest Price Per Product
prompt: A price_history table tracks how a product's price has changed over time, with columns id, product, effective_date (text), and price. A product may have many historical prices. For each product, find its current price, defined as the price with the most recent effective_date. Return product and price, ordered by product ascending.
hint: Number each product's price rows by effective_date descending and keep only row number 1.

title: Employees Tied for Top Sales in Their Branch
prompt: An employee_sales table has columns id, branch, employee, and total_sales. For each branch, find the employee (or employees, if tied) with the highest total_sales. Return branch, employee, and total_sales, ordered by branch ascending then employee ascending.
hint: Rank employees within each branch by total_sales descending and keep every row whose rank is 1.

title: Second Most Recent Order Per Customer
prompt: An orders table has columns id, customer, order_date (text), and total. For each customer, find the order placed just before their most recent order, i.e. the second most recent order. Customers with fewer than two orders should not appear in the result. Return customer, order_date, and total, ordered by customer ascending.
hint: Number each customer's orders by order_date descending and keep the row numbered 2.

title: Top Scorer for Each Team in Every Game
prompt: A game_stats table records basketball performances with columns id, game_id, team, player, and points (one row per player per game; a player belongs to one team in a given game). For every combination of game and team, find the player with the most points. If two players on the same team in the same game are tied for the most points, return the one whose name comes first alphabetically. Return game_id, team, player, and points, ordered by game_id ascending then team ascending.
hint: Partition by both game_id and team together, order by points descending, and keep row number 1.
schema_sql:
CREATE TABLE game_stats (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  game_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  team TEXT NOT NULL,
  player TEXT NOT NULL,
  points INTEGER NOT NULL
);

title: Best Two Vendors by Revenue in Each Category
prompt: A vendor_revenue table has columns id, category, vendor, and revenue, with one row per vendor per category. For each category, find the top 2 vendors by revenue. If a category has fewer than two vendors, include however many it has. Return category, vendor, and revenue, ordered by category ascending then revenue descending.
hint: Number each category's vendors by revenue descending and keep the rows numbered 1 and 2.

title: Dense Ranking of Students by GPA Within Their Grade Level
prompt: A students table has columns id, name, grade_level, and gpa. For each grade level, rank the students by gpa from highest to lowest using dense ranking: students tied on gpa receive the same rank, and the next distinct gpa gets the next consecutive rank with no gaps. Return grade_level, name, gpa, and the dense rank, ordered by grade_level ascending, then rank ascending, then name ascending.
hint: This is exactly what DENSE_RANK does when partitioned by grade_level and ordered by gpa descending.

title: Bucketing Order Sizes
prompt: A shop keeps an orders table with columns order_id (integer, primary key), customer_name (text), and total_amount (real, the order's dollar total). Classify each order into a size bucket: orders under $50 are 'Small', orders from $50 up to and including $200 are 'Medium', and anything over $200 is 'Large'. Return order_id, total_amount, and the bucket label (call it size_bucket), ordered by order_id ascending.
hint: A CASE expression with WHEN conditions checked in order from smallest to largest threshold will assign the right bucket.

title: Grading Exam Scores
prompt: A school stores exam results in a students table with columns student_id (integer, primary key), name (text), and score (integer, 0-100). Convert each score to a letter grade: 90 or above is 'A', 80-89 is 'B', 70-79 is 'C', 60-69 is 'D', and anything below 60 is 'F'. Return name, score, and grade, ordered by score descending, and for students with the same score break ties by name ascending.
hint: Check the highest threshold first in your CASE expression so it short-circuits correctly for the top grades.

title: Labeling Invoice Payment Status
prompt: A billing system tracks invoices in a table with columns invoice_id (integer, primary key), customer_name (text), due_date (text date), and paid_date (text date, NULL if the invoice has not been paid yet). Label each invoice's status: if paid_date is NULL the status is 'Unpaid'; if the invoice was paid on or before its due_date the status is 'Paid On Time'; otherwise the status is 'Paid Late'. Return invoice_id, customer_name, and status, ordered by invoice_id ascending.
hint: Test the NULL case first in your CASE expression, since comparing a NULL paid_date to due_date never evaluates true or false.

title: Pivoting Monthly Sales by Region
prompt: A sales table records transactions with columns sale_id (integer, primary key), region (text), and amount (real). Produce a single summary row that pivots total sales by region into three columns: total_east (sum of amount where region is 'East'), total_west (sum where region is 'West'), and total_north (sum where region is 'North'). Sales from any other region should be excluded from all three totals. Return exactly one row with these three columns in this order.
hint: Wrap each region's condition in a CASE inside a SUM so rows from other regions contribute zero to that column.

title: Categorizing Employee Tenure
prompt: As of January 1, 2026, an HR team wants to categorize staff tenure. The employees table has columns employee_id (integer, primary key), name (text), and hire_date (text date, format YYYY-MM-DD). Categorize each employee: hired before 2016-01-01 is 'Veteran (10+ years)', hired on or after 2016-01-01 but before 2021-01-01 is 'Experienced (5-10 years)', and hired on or after 2021-01-01 is 'New (<5 years)'. Return name, hire_date, and the category (call it tenure_category), ordered by hire_date ascending.
hint: Text dates in YYYY-MM-DD format compare correctly with ordinary <, so a CASE with two date-literal comparisons works without any date functions.

prompt: A warehouse products table has columns product_id (integer, primary key), product_name (text), and stock_quantity (integer). Label each product's stock level: exactly 0 units is 'Out of Stock', 1 to 10 units is 'Low Stock', and more than 10 units is 'In Stock'. Return product_name, stock_quantity, and the label (call it stock_label), ordered by product_id ascending.
hint: Handle the exact-zero case separately from the low-quantity range in your CASE expression.

title: Classifying Customer Spend Tiers
prompt: A customers table has columns customer_id (integer, primary key) and name (text). An orders table has columns order_id (integer, primary key), customer_id (integer), and amount (real). Compute each customer's total spend (treat a customer with no orders as spending 0) and assign a tier: 1000 or more is 'Gold', 500 up to but not including 1000 is 'Silver', and anything below 500 (including 0) is 'Bronze'. Return name, total_spend, and tier, ordered by total_spend descending, breaking ties by name ascending.
hint: Use a LEFT JOIN with COALESCE so customers without orders still show up with a spend of 0, then apply CASE to the aggregated total.

title: Marking Late Shipments
prompt: An orders table tracks fulfillment with columns order_id (integer, primary key), order_date (text date), ship_date (text date, NULL if not yet shipped), and expected_ship_days (integer, how many days the order is allowed to take to ship). Determine each order's shipping status: if ship_date is NULL the status is 'Not Shipped'; otherwise, if the number of days between order_date and ship_date is less than or equal to expected_ship_days the status is 'On Time', and otherwise it is 'Late'. Return order_id and status, ordered by order_id ascending.
hint: Compute the day gap with julianday(ship_date) - julianday(order_date) and check the NULL ship_date case first in your CASE expression.

title: Rating Movie Reviews
prompt: A reviews table stores movie ratings with columns review_id (integer, primary key), movie_title (text), and rating (integer, 1 to 5). Classify each review as 'Positive' (rating 4 or 5), 'Neutral' (rating 3), or 'Negative' (rating 1 or 2), then return a single summary row with the count of reviews in each category as three columns: positive_count, neutral_count, negative_count.
hint: Sum a CASE that evaluates to 1 or 0 for each category to turn row-level classification into a count.

title: Segmenting Age Groups
prompt: A customers table has columns customer_id (integer, primary key), name (text), and age (integer). Segment customers into four age groups: under 18 is 'Minor', 18 to 35 inclusive is 'Young Adult', 36 to 55 inclusive is 'Middle Aged', and over 55 is 'Senior'. Return a single summary row with the count of customers in each group as four columns, in this order: minor_count, young_adult_count, middle_aged_count, senior_count.
hint: BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends, which lines up neatly with the inclusive age ranges here.

title: Highlighting Price Changes
prompt: A price_history table logs price changes with columns id (integer, primary key), product_name (text), old_price (real), and new_price (real). Label each row's movement: 'Increase' if new_price is greater than old_price, 'Decrease' if new_price is less than old_price, and 'No Change' if they are equal. Return product_name, old_price, new_price, and the label (call it change_label), ordered by id ascending.
hint: A CASE expression comparing the two price columns directly covers all three outcomes without needing a subtraction.

title: Tagging Attendance Status
prompt: An attendance table logs classroom check-ins with columns id (integer, primary key), student_name (text), class_start_time (text, HH:MM), and check_in_time (text, HH:MM, NULL if the student never checked in). Tag each record: NULL check_in_time is 'Absent'; a check_in_time at or before class_start_time is 'On Time'; anything after is 'Late'. Return student_name and status, ordered by id ascending.
hint: HH:MM strings compare correctly with ordinary text comparison operators, so check the NULL case first and then compare the two time columns directly.

title: Employees Earning More Than Their Manager
prompt: Table employees(id, name, manager_id, salary) stores every employee. manager_id references another employee's id (it is NULL for the employee at the top of the hierarchy who has no manager). Find every employee whose salary is strictly greater than their own manager's salary. Return the employee's name and their manager's name, ordered by employee name ascending.
hint: Join the employees table to itself, matching each employee's manager_id to another row's id.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, manager_id INTEGER, salary INTEGER);

title: Skip-Level Reporting Pairs
prompt: Table employees(id, name, manager_id) stores every employee, where manager_id references another employee's id (NULL at the top of the hierarchy). For every employee who has both a manager and a 'skip-level' manager (their manager's own manager), return the employee's name and the skip-level manager's name, ordered by employee name ascending.
hint: Join the employees table to itself twice: once to find each employee's manager, and again to find that manager's manager.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, manager_id INTEGER);

title: Managers With More Than Two Direct Reports
prompt: Table employees(id, name, manager_id) stores every employee, where manager_id references the id of that employee's manager (NULL if they have none). Find every manager who has more than 2 direct reports. Return the manager's name and the count of their direct reports, ordered by manager name ascending.
hint: Self join employees to their direct reports, then group by the manager and filter the group counts with HAVING.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, manager_id INTEGER);

title: Same-Department Colleague Pairs
prompt: Table employees(id, name, department) stores every employee. Find every unique pair of distinct employees who work in the same department, listing each pair only once (never pair an employee with themselves, and never list both orderings of the same pair). Return the two employee names, with the alphabetically earlier name first, plus the shared department. Order by department ascending, then the first employee name ascending, then the second employee name ascending.
hint: Self join employees on matching department, using a strict name-inequality condition to keep each pair only once.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, department TEXT);

title: Products Sharing the Same Price
prompt: Table products(id, name, price) stores the catalog. Find every pair of distinct products that have exactly the same price, listing each pair only once (never pair a product with itself, and never list both orderings of the same pair — use the product ids to decide which name comes first in each pair). Return the two product names plus the shared price. Order by price ascending, then the first product name ascending, then the second product name ascending.
hint: Self join products on matching price, using an id-inequality condition to keep each pair only once.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, price REAL);

title: Employees Hired on the Same Day
prompt: Table employees(id, name, hire_date) stores every employee, with hire_date as a 'YYYY-MM-DD' text value. Find every pair of distinct employees who were hired on the exact same date, listing each pair only once (never pair an employee with themselves, and never list both orderings of the same pair — use the employee ids to decide which name comes first in each pair). Return the two employee names plus the shared hire_date. Order by hire_date ascending, then the first employee name ascending, then the second employee name ascending.
hint: Self join employees on matching hire_date, using an id-inequality condition to keep each pair only once.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, hire_date TEXT);

title: Round-Trip Flight Routes
prompt: Table flights(id, origin, destination, flight_number) stores scheduled flights. A route has a 'return flight' if some other flight travels the opposite direction (destination back to origin). Find every flight that has such a matching return flight, but only report each city pair once: keep the flight whose origin comes alphabetically before its destination. Return the flight_number, origin, and destination, ordered by origin ascending, then destination ascending.
hint: Join the flights table to itself, matching one flight's origin/destination to the other's destination/origin in reverse.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE flights (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, origin TEXT, destination TEXT, flight_number TEXT);

title: Reciprocal Follow Pairs
prompt: Table users(id, name) lists app users, and table follows(follower_id, followee_id) records that follower_id follows followee_id. Two users have a 'reciprocal follow' if each follows the other. Find every reciprocal pair, reporting each pair only once: put the user whose name is alphabetically first as the first column and the other user as the second column. Return the two user names, ordered by the first name ascending, then the second name ascending.
hint: Self join the follows table on itself with follower and followee swapped to detect mutual pairs, then join to users for names and filter to keep each pair once.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE follows (follower_id INTEGER, followee_id INTEGER);

title: Users With Consecutive Login Days
prompt: Table logins(id, user_name, login_date) records one row per login, with login_date as a 'YYYY-MM-DD' text value. Find every case where the same user logged in on two calendar days in a row (one login_date is exactly one day after another for that user). Return the user_name and the earlier of the two dates for each such consecutive pair, ordered by user_name ascending, then the earlier date ascending.
hint: Self join logins on matching user_name where one row's date, plus one day, equals the other row's date.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE logins (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, user_name TEXT, login_date TEXT);

title: Meeting Room Double Bookings
prompt: Table meetings(id, room, start_time, end_time) stores booked meetings, with start_time and end_time as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM' text values that sort correctly as text. Two meetings in the same room overlap if one starts before the other ends, and that other one also starts before the first one ends. Find every pair of distinct meetings in the same room whose times overlap, listing each pair only once (use the meeting ids to decide which comes first in each pair). Return the two meeting ids plus the room, ordered by room ascending, then the first meeting id ascending, then the second meeting id ascending.
hint: Self join meetings on matching room with an id-inequality to keep each pair once, then compare start/end times to test for overlap.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE meetings (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, room TEXT, start_time TEXT, end_time TEXT);

title: Same Title, Different Department
prompt: Table employees(id, name, department, title) stores every employee. Find every pair of distinct employees who hold the same job title but work in different departments, listing each pair only once (use the employee ids to decide which name comes first in each pair). Return the two employee names plus the shared title, ordered by title ascending, then the first employee name ascending, then the second employee name ascending.
hint: Self join employees on matching title with both a department-inequality and an id-inequality condition.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, department TEXT, title TEXT);

title: Students Sharing a Birthday
prompt: Table students(id, name, birth_date) stores each student's birth_date as a 'YYYY-MM-DD' text value. Find every pair of distinct students who share the same birthday, meaning the same month and day regardless of birth year, listing each pair only once (use the student ids to decide which name comes first in each pair). Return the two student names plus the shared month-day formatted as 'MM-DD', ordered by the month-day ascending, then the first student name ascending, then the second student name ascending.
hint: Self join students on the month-and-day portion of birth_date (extractable with strftime('%m-%d', birth_date)), using an id-inequality to keep each pair once.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, birth_date TEXT);

title: Monthly Revenue Growth by Category
prompt: A retailer logs individual sales with a category, a sale month (text like '2024-01'), and an amount. For each category and each month that appears in the data, compute the total revenue for that category-month, and the growth in revenue compared to the previous month that appears for that category (previous total subtracted from current total). If a category-month has no earlier month on record for that category, its growth should be NULL. Return category, sale_month, total_revenue, and growth, ordered by category ascending and then sale_month ascending.
hint: Aggregate revenue per category-month in one CTE, then use LAG over a second CTE partitioned by category and ordered by month to get the previous total.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE sales (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, category TEXT, sale_month TEXT, amount INTEGER);

title: Repeat Customers This Quarter
prompt: A store logs each order with the customer name, the fiscal quarter it fell in (values like '2024-Q1'), and an amount. Find customers who placed two or more orders during quarter '2024-Q1' specifically. Return customer_name and their order_count for that quarter, ordered by order_count descending, then customer_name ascending.
hint: Stage just the '2024-Q1' orders in one CTE, then group and filter with HAVING in a second.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_name TEXT, quarter TEXT, amount INTEGER);

title: Department Runner-Up Salaries
prompt: A company stores employees with their department and salary. For each department, find the employee(s) earning the second-highest distinct salary in that department (the runner-up), not the top earner. If a department has fewer than two distinct salary values, exclude it entirely. Return department, name, and salary, ordered by department ascending, then name ascending.
hint: Use DENSE_RANK over salary within each department in one CTE, then filter for rank 2 in a second.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, department TEXT, salary INTEGER);

title: Products Never Discounted

title: Orders Above Customer's Own Average
prompt: An orders table records each order's customer name, order date, and amount. For each customer, find their individual orders whose amount is strictly greater than that same customer's own average order amount, computed across all of their orders. Return customer_name, order_date, and amount for every qualifying order, ordered by customer_name ascending, then order_date ascending.
hint: Compute each customer's average order amount in one CTE, then join it back to the orders and filter where amount exceeds that customer's average.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_name TEXT, order_date TEXT, amount INTEGER);

title: Time Between First and Last Purchase per Customer
prompt: A purchases table records each purchase's customer name and purchase date (text in YYYY-MM-DD form). For each customer, compute the number of days between their very first purchase and their very last purchase. Only include customers who have made two or more purchases (a customer with a single purchase has nothing to measure and should be excluded). Return customer_name, first_purchase_date, last_purchase_date, and days_between as an integer, ordered by customer_name ascending.
hint: Get each customer's MIN and MAX purchase date (and a count) in one CTE, then filter to customers with 2+ purchases and compute the date difference in a second CTE.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE purchases (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_name TEXT, purchase_date TEXT);

title: Categories With Above-Average Product Price
prompt: A products table lists each product's name, category, and price. Find every category whose average product price is higher than the average price across all products in the entire catalog. Return category and avg_price, ordered by avg_price descending.
hint: Compute each category's average price in one CTE and the overall catalog average in a second CTE, then compare them.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product_name TEXT, category TEXT, price INTEGER);

title: Late Shipment Rate by Warehouse
prompt: A shipments table records, for each shipment, which warehouse it shipped from and whether it arrived late (is_late = 1) or on time (is_late = 0). For each warehouse, compute the late rate as the number of late shipments divided by total shipments, expressed as a percentage rounded to one decimal place. Only include warehouses with at least 3 total shipments on record. Return warehouse and late_rate_pct, ordered by late_rate_pct descending, then warehouse ascending.
hint: Tally total and late shipment counts per warehouse in one CTE, then compute and filter the percentage in a second CTE.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE shipments (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, warehouse TEXT, is_late INTEGER);

title: Top Selling Product in Each Region
prompt: A sales table records transactions with a region, a product name, and units sold. For each region, find the product with the highest total units sold, summed across all its transactions in that region. If multiple products tie for the highest total in a region, include all of them. Return region, product_name, and total_units, ordered by region ascending, then product_name ascending.
hint: Sum units sold per region and product in one CTE, then rank products within each region by that total in a second CTE and keep rank 1.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE sales (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT, product_name TEXT, units_sold INTEGER);

title: Customers Who Upgraded Their Subscription Tier
prompt: A subscription_events table logs an event each time a customer's tier changes, with the customer name, event date, and the new numeric tier level (higher numbers mean a better tier). For each customer, compare each event to that customer's immediately preceding event (ordered by date), and find every event where the tier increased compared to the previous event -- an upgrade. Return customer_name, event_date, tier (the new tier), and previous_tier, ordered by customer_name ascending then event_date ascending.
hint: Use LAG partitioned by customer and ordered by event_date in one CTE to get each event's previous tier, then filter for increases in a second CTE.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE subscription_events (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_name TEXT, event_date TEXT, tier INTEGER);

title: Running Total of Weekly Signups
prompt: A signups table logs new user signups, with each row giving a week label (like '2024-W01') and the number of new users recorded (a week can have multiple rows if signups were logged in separate batches). Compute, for each week, the total new users that week and the cumulative running total of new users through that week (summing that week and all earlier weeks, ordered by week label). Return signup_week, weekly_total, and running_total, ordered by signup_week ascending.
hint: Sum new_users per week in one CTE, then apply a running SUM window function ordered by week in a second CTE.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE signups (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, signup_week TEXT, new_users INTEGER);
